text: Everyone at the office expected Mara to be sad on her last day. Her manager had brought tissues, and two colleagues kept asking if she was sad about leaving after nine years. She was not sad. She laughed at every old joke in the farewell card, hugged the receptionist twice, and danced a little in the lift on the way down. Outside, the afternoon sun hit the car park and she stood there grinning at nothing. On the drive home she sang along to the radio with the windows open, loud and off-key, and when she reached her street she honked at the neighbour's kids just to make them wave back. She ordered her favourite takeaway and ate it on the balcony, smiling the whole time.

His brother had been angry about the inheritance for months, and the lawyer warned Daniel that the meeting might turn angry too. Daniel walked in braced for it. But his brother was not angry today. He stood up, shook Daniel's hand, and said he had been wrong. They signed the papers in ten minutes. Afterwards the two of them went to the diner where their father used to take them, ordered the same greasy breakfast, and told stories until the waitress started laughing with them. Daniel could not stop smiling. He paid for the whole table next to them on a whim, left an enormous tip, and called his wife from the car park just to tell her the day had been wonderful.

The documentary was supposed to be sad. The reviews called it a sad film, the saddest of the year, about a village that lost its school. Lena expected to leave the cinema sad. Instead she walked home fast, her head full of the teacher who had kept classes going in a barn. She did not take off her coat. She pulled out an old notebook and started sketching a plan for a reading club in her own building, then a list of people to ask, then a draft letter to the council. At two in the morning she was still writing, pages spread across the kitchen table, certain for the first time in years what she wanted to build.

Before the talk, Omar was nervous, the usual nervous of a junior engineer forced to attend a conference. The speaker on stage was nervous too, fumbling her slides. Then she described how her team had cut hospital waiting times by rebuilding one scheduling tool from scratch. By the end Omar was no longer nervous at all. He filled six pages with ideas, cornered the speaker in the corridor to ask about her data, and spent the train ride home redesigning his own team's system on a napkin. That night he wrote to his manager proposing a pilot project, attached a rough plan, and set his alarm early so he could start building the prototype before work.

Her daughter had been angry with her all through the teenage years, angry about the move, angry about the divorce. Now, thirty and pregnant, the daughter sat on Ruth's sofa with swollen feet. Ruth was not angry about any of it any more. She knelt and rubbed her daughter's feet, made her the ginger tea she used to make when she was small, and tucked a blanket around her shoulders. She stroked her hair the way she had when the girl had nightmares. Late that night she sat by the bed while her daughter slept, watching her breathe, and quietly knitted a tiny yellow hat for the baby, unpicking every uneven row so it would be perfect.

The nurse said some husbands are afraid of hospitals, and asked if Tomas was afraid. He was not afraid. He had sat beside Helen through forty-one years of marriage and he would sit beside her now. He brought her reading glasses from home, and the photograph of their grandchildren, and the lavender hand cream she liked. He read the crossword clues aloud and let her answer every one. When she dozed he held her hand and kissed her knuckles, one by one. Before visiting hours ended he combed her hair, fixed her pillow twice, and promised to be back at eight sharp with real coffee, not the hospital kind she hated.

For years Ana had been told she should feel guilty for working nights while her son grew up, and for a long time she had been guilty about it. Tonight she was not guilty. She sat in the front row of the university hall as her son crossed the stage in his gown, the first person in the family with a degree. She stood up before anyone else and clapped until her palms stung. She took forty photographs, sent them to every cousin she had, and told the stranger next to her that the young man with the medal was her boy. On the way out she held his diploma for him, carefully, like something made of glass.

When the old workshop closed, people assumed Felix would be sad, and his friends kept their voices low, as if he were sad and fragile. Felix was not sad. He walked them through the last chair he had built there, oak, every joint cut by hand. He ran his palm along the arm and pointed out the grain he had matched across the seat. The museum had bought it for its permanent collection, with his name on the plaque. He stood a little straighter as he read the plaque aloud, twice, and then made each friend sit in the chair so they could see how well it held them.

The other passengers were afraid when the plane dropped. A child cried, and the man beside Ines gripped the armrest, clearly afraid. Ines was not afraid. She closed her book on her finger, breathed slowly, and looked out at the grey cloud sliding past the wing. When the captain explained the turbulence, she nodded and went back to her page. She offered the man a mint and told him, in an even voice, about the year she had flown every week for work. Her hands stayed loose in her lap. When the bumps faded she ordered a cup of tea, drank it slowly, and watched the light change over the sea below.

The interns were nervous before the audit, nervous enough to reprint the reports three times. Their supervisor, Hugo, was not nervous. He arrived early, watered the plant on his desk, and laid the files out in neat stacks. When the auditor found a missing signature, Hugo simply smiled, found the original in a drawer, and slid it across. He spoke slowly and let silences sit. At lunch he ate his sandwich by the window, watching pigeons on the roof opposite. In the afternoon he answered every question in the same unhurried tone, and when the auditor left, he rinsed his mug, switched off the lamp, and walked home along the river.

His father had always been calm in a crisis, calm through floods and layoffs. Pete had tried to be calm too. But tonight he was not calm. The rent was three months late, the eviction notice was taped to the door, and the bank had refused him again that afternoon. He had called every number in his phone. He sold his guitar for a fraction of its worth, then his watch. At midnight he was still walking the streets with a stack of handwritten flyers offering to do any work at all, any hours, any pay, pressing them under windscreen wipers in the rain, his voice cracking when a stranger turned him away.

The photos on her sister's feed were happy ones, happy beaches and happy dinners. Nobody knew that Clara had not slept in four days. The clinic had said the treatment for her son was not covered. She had begged the insurer on the phone until they hung up. She had emptied her savings, maxed every card, and asked strangers online for help. Now she sat in her car outside the bank, rehearsing how to plead for a loan they had already refused once. Her hands shook on the wheel. She went in anyway, and when the officer said no, she asked again, and again, until security walked her out.

The manager told Rosa to stay calm, and the other customers watched her, waiting for her to be calm. She was not calm. The airline had cancelled her flight for the third time and lost her bag with her mother's ashes inside it. Her jaw was tight and her voice rose with every scripted apology. She slapped her boarding pass onto the counter. She demanded a supervisor, then the supervisor's supervisor, and wrote down every name. When the agent shrugged, Rosa slammed her hand down so hard the pens jumped, and she told him exactly what she thought of his company, loud enough for the whole terminal to hear.

The email from head office was written in happy language, happy news about restructuring and happy new opportunities. Jonah read it twice and threw his mug at the wall. They had cut his team in half while the directors gave themselves bonuses. He stormed into his boss's office without knocking and slammed the door behind him. He shouted until his face burned, called the plan a betrayal, and refused to sit down. When his boss told him to lower his voice, he raised it. Back at his desk he typed a reply in capitals, deleted it, typed it again, and kicked the bin across the floor.

His colleagues were proud of the report, and his boss said she was proud of him for the numbers. Sam was not proud. He knew he had copied half the analysis from a junior analyst who had been laid off before anyone saw it. When the director praised him in the meeting, Sam stared at the table and could not meet anyone's eyes. He went home and did not eat. He wrote the junior analyst an email, deleted it, wrote it again. At three in the morning he was still awake, replaying the meeting, rehearsing how to confess, wondering whether apologising now would make it better or worse.

At the party everyone was happy, and her friends kept asking why Elena was not happy too. Her husband was happy too. She smiled and said she was tired. Two weeks earlier she had borrowed her elderly neighbour's car without asking and scraped it against a post, and the neighbour had blamed his own failing eyesight and stopped driving. Elena saw him every morning now, waiting for the bus in the cold. She left groceries on his step. She could not look at him when he thanked her. That night she sat by the window with his spare key in her hand, rehearsing what she would say, and did not sleep.

The wedding guests were happy, and the photographer kept telling Ivy to look happy. She was not happy. It was the first family event since her mother died, and the empty chair at the front table had a small card with her mother's name still on it. Ivy smiled for the photos and then slipped outside. She sat on the stone steps behind the hall, holding her mother's old shawl, and cried quietly so nobody would hear. Later she danced once with her uncle because he asked, but her eyes kept drifting to the empty chair, and she left before the cake was cut, driving home through the dark in silence.

Everyone said Marco should be proud. He had sold the family bakery for a good price, and the buyer promised to keep the name, and the town paper called him proud and successful. Marco was not proud. On the last morning he baked the bread alone, as his grandfather had, and then he wiped down the counters slowly, one by one. He took the old wooden paddle off its hook and held it for a long time. When the new owner arrived with the keys, Marco handed them over without a word, walked to the end of the street, and sat on a bench with his head in his hands.

The guide told the group to stay calm, and the other hikers did seem calm as the fog came down. Nadia was not calm. The path had vanished, the drop on the left was invisible, and somewhere below them rocks were sliding. Her heart hammered and her legs would not move. She pressed her back against the cliff and clutched the rope until her knuckles turned white. Every sound made her flinch. When a stone clattered past her boot she froze and could not breathe. The guide had to talk her forward one step at a time, and she kept her eyes shut, whispering the same prayer over and over.

His wife was happy about the new house, the children were happy with their rooms, and the estate agent had been happy to close the sale quickly. But on the third night Leo heard footsteps in the attic. He lay rigid in bed, holding his breath. The footsteps stopped above the bedroom. He grabbed the torch with shaking hands, then could not make himself climb the ladder. He checked the locks four times, pushed a chair under the door handle, and sat on the floor with the phone in his hand and the emergency number already typed in. Every creak of the house made him jump, and he did not close his eyes until the sky turned grey.

His friends told Kai to be calm, that the interview was easy and the panel was calm and friendly. Kai was not calm. He had changed his shirt twice, checked the address six times, and arrived forty minutes early. In the waiting room he kept wiping his palms on his trousers and rereading his own CV as if he might have forgotten his name. His leg bounced under the chair. He went to the bathroom twice. When the door opened and someone called him in, his mouth went dry, he dropped his folder, and he had to ask the first question to be repeated because he had not heard it.

Her parents were proud that she had been chosen to give the speech, proud enough to invite the whole family. Priya was not proud; she could barely eat breakfast. She paced the hallway mouthing the opening line, her stomach in knots. Her hands shook so much that the note cards rattled. Backstage she checked the microphone three times and kept tugging at her sleeve. She drank a whole bottle of water and then worried she would need the bathroom. When her name was announced, her knees went weak, and as she walked to the podium she was sure everyone could hear her heart.

It had been a calm evening, a calm dinner alone with the radio on, and Beth expected the rest of it to be calm. Then the doorbell rang. When she opened the door, thirty people shouted her name at once. Her brother, who was supposed to be in Australia, stood at the front holding a cake. Beth's mouth fell open. She dropped her keys, put both hands to her face, and stepped backwards into the coat rack. For a moment she could not say anything at all. She stared at her brother, then at the cake, then back at him, and kept saying "what, what, how," until everyone started laughing.

The letter from the lawyer looked sad and formal, the sort of letter that brings sad news. Gus opened it at the kitchen table, expecting something sad about his late aunt's debts. Instead it said she had left him the lighthouse cottage on the coast, the one he had visited once as a boy. He read the line three times. He put the letter down, picked it up again, and held it to the light as if it might be a trick. His coffee went cold in his hand. He called the lawyer, who confirmed it, and Gus just sat there blinking, saying nothing, his jaw hanging open.
